visuals.title: Where MND strikes
visuals.text: Motor neurons in the brain and spinal cord; bulbar muscles of the throat and the breathing muscles fail.

visuals.title: Excitotoxicity and riluzole
visuals.text: Riluzole is antiglutamatergic, slowing this cycle a little.

glossary.Neurodegenerative: Describes diseases where nerve cells progressively die and are not replaced.
glossary.Motor neurons: Nerve cells that carry movement commands from the brain and spinal cord to muscles.
glossary.Wasting: Visible loss of muscle bulk, a lower motor neuron sign.
glossary.Spinal ALS: ALS that starts with limb weakness rather than speech or swallowing problems.
glossary.Bulbar ALS: ALS starting in the bulbar muscles, causing slurred speech and swallowing difficulty first.
glossary.Upgoing plantar: Big toe extends upwards when the sole is stroked; an upper motor neuron sign.
glossary.Brisk reflexes: Exaggerated tendon reflexes, an upper motor neuron sign.
glossary.Absent reflexes: No tendon reflex response, a lower motor neuron sign.
glossary.Distal phalanx: The tip bone of a finger or toe.
glossary.Tongue fasciculations: Visible flickering twitches of the tongue at rest from lower motor neuron damage.
glossary.Respiratory failure: Lungs cannot keep blood oxygen up or carbon dioxide down; in MND from weak breathing muscles.
glossary.Cranial nerves: Twelve nerve pairs from the brainstem supplying the head and neck; IX, X and XII control swallowing and tongue.
glossary.Median survival: The time by which half of patients have died.
glossary.Atrophy: Shrinking of a tissue, here muscle, from loss of nerve supply.
glossary.Familial: Running in families because of an inherited gene change.
glossary.Nerve conduction studies: Test measuring how fast and strongly electrical signals travel along nerves.
glossary.MRI: Magnetic resonance imaging; detailed scan used here to exclude spinal cord compression.
glossary.Disease-modifying: A treatment that changes the course of the disease, not just the symptoms.
glossary.Antiglutamatergic: Reduces the release or effect of the excitatory messenger glutamate.
glossary.Physiotherapy: Therapy using exercise and movement to keep function and prevent contractures.
glossary.Speech and language therapy: Therapy helping communication and safe swallowing.
glossary.Nutritional support: Measures to keep up calorie intake, such as diet changes or tube feeding.
glossary.Gain-of-function: A mutation making a protein do something new and harmful, rather than stop working.
glossary.Superoxide dismutase: Enzyme that neutralises damaging oxygen free radicals; coded by SOD1.
glossary.Synapse: Junction where one nerve cell passes a chemical signal to another cell.
glossary.Oculomotor: Relating to the nerves and muscles that move the eyes.
glossary.Sensory pathways: Nerve routes carrying touch, pain, temperature and position sense to the brain.
glossary.Descending inhibitory control: Signals from the brain that calm spinal reflexes; their loss causes spasticity and brisk reflexes.
glossary.Cranial nerve nuclei: Clusters of nerve cells in the brainstem from which cranial nerves arise.
glossary.Muscle fibres: The individual contracting cells that make up a muscle.
glossary.Mixed UMN and LMN signs: Upper and lower motor neuron signs together in the same patient, typical of ALS.
